Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP Victorian politics Victorian microparty MPs including Georgie Purcell to face re-election struggle after group voting tickets abolished Voters will be required to number at least five parties above the line in order of preference after bill passed upper house 33 votes to four Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Benita Kolovos Victorian state correspondent Wed 12 Aug 2026 02.15 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 02.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Prominent MPs such as Georgie Purcell and other microparty members will face an uphill battle to retain their seats in Victoria’s upper house after parliament voted to abolish group voting tickets. Victoria’s legislative council was the only remaining upper house in Australia to use the GVT system, in which voters could only choose one party above the line on the ballot paper, with their preferences then allocated by the party if it was knocked out during counting. But the electoral amendment (miscellaneous matters) bill 2026 passed the upper house on Tuesday night – 33 votes to four – which will mean GVTs cannot be used in the November state election. Instead, voters will be required to number at least five parties above the line in order of preference. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The GVT system has long been criticised by experts, including election analyst Antony Green, as they allow backroom deals between parties to flourish and enable some candidates to get elected with a small number of primary votes. “This reform is about converting the electoral system into one that rewards parties that get votes over parties who, in the past, have been elected by clever preference deals,” Green told Guardian Australia on Wednesday. “In the last decade we’ve had about 20 candidates elected with under 6% of the vote – some as low as 1% – who’ve defeated candidates with many more votes because of these preference deals. “That is impossible under a system where voters control their own preferences.” The four MPs who opposed the bill were Purcell, who leads the Animal Justice party; the Legalise Cannabis MP Rachel Payne; the Libertarian MP David Limbrick; and the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers MP Jeff Bourman. Ben Raue, an electoral analyst and founder of the Tally Room, said the four MPs represented parties that had benefited from GVTs and were “going to have a lot of trouble getting someone elected with this new system”. “That’s unfortunate for them. But ultimately this about whether GVTs are a fair way to run a democracy and I don’t think it is,” he said. “Voters should have control of their preferences.” Purcell said the changes “significantly decrease” her chances of being re-elected but that “it’s not over until it’s over”. “My team and I are dedicated to running a strong campaign and doing everything we can to secure another four years in parliament,” she said. Payne and Limbrick have also committed to running again, with the latter – who was a prominent critic of the government’s Covid-19 measures – describing his party as “underdogs”. “No one had heard of us when I was elected in 2018, I was written off in 2022 and quadrupled my vote, and they are writing us off again in 2026,” he said. The trio said they supported abolishing GVTs but only if the government also scrapped the state’s eight upper-house regions and replaced them with a single statewide electorate of 40 seats. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion That would lower the electoral quota from 16.7% to 2.4% if members were elected every four years or about 4.8% for eight-year terms. However, such a change would require a referendum. A parliamentary inquiry examining GVTs last year recommended they be abolished in time for the 2026 election and proposed holding a referendum on broader structural reform in 2028 or 2030. Payne said abolishing GVTs without broader reform “benefits the major parties rather than strengthening our democracy”. “This reform is self-serving and motivated by all the wrong reasons,” she said. Based on statewide polling, Green expects the Coalition could win two seats in each region under the new system. Labor could win two seats in some regions and be reduced to one in others. He said Greens could win up to six seats – one in every metropolitan region and possibly one in the regions – while One Nation could win eight or nine seats. Green stressed that would happen “with or without group voting tickets”, given the party is polling at about 20% of the primary vote. “Whatever happens, if the Liberal party form government after the election, even with a majority, they will not have a majority in the upper house,” he said. “They will have to rely on One Nation in the upper house.” Explore more on these topics Victorian politics Victoria news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Victoria’s voice to parliament asks government to axe bill that will scrap prisoners’ ‘open air’ rights Victoria had bipartisan support for a legal right to work from home. Image: Jerry Lampen/REUTERS Advertisement More than 30 years after the end of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina (1992-1995), Srebrenica remains emblematic of its brutality. And no one is more closely linked to the genocide that took place in the small town in eastern Bosnia than Ratko Mladic , the former commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb army. Although the United Nations had declared Srebrenica a "safe area," Bosnian Serb forces attacked the town. Within just a few days in July 1995, they expelled women and children, then killed more than 8,300 unarmed Muslim boys and men in the nearby village of Potocari — on Mladic's direct orders, according to the verdict handed down by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague 22 years later. At the time, Srebrenica was the largest massacre in Europe since World War II . The ICTY classified it as genocide. Mladic was also held responsible for other war crimes beyond the Srebrenica genocide. Under his command, the years-long siege of Sarajevo began at the start of the war. The city was shelled for more than 40 months, killing around 11,000 people, including more than 1,600 children. Mladic always claimed that he targeted only military objectives. But numerous reports and intercepted radio communications indicate that civilian facilities and residential areas were also deliberately attacked. Around 100,000 people were killed during the four-year war in Bosnia, while some 2.2 million were driven from their homes in cities and villages across the country, half of its total population at the time. Former Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic dead To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video 'The butcher of the Balkans' In 2017, Mladic was sentenced to life in prison by the tribunal in The Hague. International media dubbed him "the Butcher of the Balkans." He was found responsible for some of the most serious war crimes and the genocide committed during the Bosnian War. Mladic consistently denied any responsibility. He saw himself as an avenger of the Serbs for centuries of Ottoman rule in the Balkans, and viewed Bosnia's Muslims, who today call themselves Bosniaks, as direct descendants of the Turks. In front of his soldiers, he referred to them simply as "the Turks" and showed no empathy. "Borders are always drawn with blood, and states are marked with graves," he is quoted as saying. Bosnia-Herzegovina: 30 years after Srebrenica massacre To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Career in the Yugoslav army At the beginning of the Croatian War in June 1991, when Serbs living in Croatia rose up against the independence of the former Yugoslav republic with active support from Serbia, Mladic's role fundamentall changed. As a colonel in the Yugoslav army, he became commander of the 9th Corps in the Croatian city of Knin. His task was to organize Serb militias and support them in their fight against Croatian independence. Under Mladic's command, the Croatian cities of Sibenik and Zadar were bombarded, and Croatian civilians were driven from surrounding towns and villages. In May 1992, he took on the same role in Bosnia. By then promoted to general, Mladic became commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb forces, seeking to establish a territorial link between Serb-held areas in the east and west of the former Yugoslav republic. Ratko Mladic (left) and Radovan Karadzic, the political leader of the Bosnian Serbs during the Bosnian War, on August 5, 1993. Image: picture-alliance/ dpa Flight, arrest and final verdict At the height of his career, Colonel General Ratko Mladic was a fervent Serbian nationalist. But he began his career as a committed communist. Born in eastern Bosnia in 1943, Mladic was just two years old when his father, one of Tito's Partisans, was killed by fascist Croatian Ustasha militia. The loss is often described as a formative influence, shaping his later worldview. As a young man, Mladic embarked on a military career, attending the Military Academy in Belgrade. He later graduated at the top of his class. He quickly rose through the ranks of the Yugoslav army, which for many years was regarded as one of the most stable institutions in the multiethnic state. Serbian nationalist Before the end of the Bosnian War in late 1995, Mladic was indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. But he evaded arrest for years. Supported by networks within the Serbian military and political establishment, he lived largely undisturbed underground and was even seen in public. He was finally arrested in 2011, after 16 years on the run and mounting international pressure. The subsequent trial in The Hague lasted a total of 523 days. Nearly 600 witnesses testified, while numerous documents and other pieces of evidence were examined. Mladic was ultimately sentenced to life in prison at trial, among other charges for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. In 2021, an appeals chamber upheld the verdict, making it final. Legally, this established his responsibility as one of the principal figures behind the crimes committed during the Bosnian War. Ratko Mladic life sentence upheld To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video A war criminal who saw himself as a hero Internationally, the verdict was hailed as historic. United Nations officials saw it as a signal that accountability can still be pursued decades after crimes are committed. For many survivors and relatives of the victims, the verdict was a long-overdue but important acknowledgment of their suffering. Mladic himself, however, remained defiant to the end. Throughout the trial, he maintained that he was innocent, calling the charges against him "disgusting" and the tribunal "satanic." Many of his supporters in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs still see him as a hero. While he is regarded internationally as a war criminal, his admirers continue to portray him as a defender of Serbian interests and a hero — even painting his likeness on walls. While he was still on the run, Mladic threatened his pursuers, claiming he always carried a poison pill and that he would never be captured alive. But he never swallowed the pill during his decades in hiding. He survived several strokes while in prison. Ratko Mladic died on August 27, 2026, at the prison hospital in The Hague at the age of 84.
